summary: "Orbital RUSH!" is a two-player physical board game where players design, launch, and fly a Mars orbiter under real engineering limits. Each player draws a budget, chooses an orbiter, fills its limited payload slot with "chip" components such as: solar panels, antennas, and science instruments inspired by real NASA missions. Players roll dice for launch, and then race along a route to Mars while event cards based on real spacecraft problems test their design. Costs, masses, travel times, and hazards are scaled from NASA mission data, so players experience the trade-offs of mission design with no coding or special equipment.
details:
"Orbiter RUSH!" lets people imagine and experience what it is like to run a mission. The game is targeted mostly at children, so we made the game simple for easy understanding for younger players, but there are no such rules for older people to be able to play the game. We want to help people gain a vision of, or feel the slightest intrigue about, space missions while gaining knowledge and having fun!

Each player draws a budget card, selects an orbiter (from very small, small, medium, large, or experimental). Players then purchase "chip" components such as solar panels, an antenna, fuel, and science instruments, all based on real NASA missions. These components must fit inside the orbiter’s limited payload bay, forcing players to make strategic decisions based on mass, cost, power, and communication needs. Science instruments only score points if the orbiter also carries a solar panel, an antenna, and fuel.

At launch, players roll two dice, where a low roll can damage components. Players then navigate a route with checkpoints, drawing event cards based on real spacecraft problems (micrometeoroid hits, solar storms, stuck antennas, communication blackouts).  Upon reaching Mars, players can add up their science points, and the highest score wins. (More detailed rules and conditions are in the Project Demonstration.)

Benefits that come in our game consist of:

  • Players learn how real mission designers balance budget, mass, power, and communications, without needing any experience.
  • It needs no coding, screens, or internet, so it can be played in classrooms, homes, or anywhere with limited technology.
  • Most numbers and events are traceable to NASA or other public sources. Almost all cards have the source, so players can look up the real missions themselves.
  • A single game takes up 10-15 minutes to play, which makes it easy to use in a lesson.

We hope to make mission design more understandable and enjoyable for students and beginners. Through the game, players can experience how spacecraft are built under real-world limits, and how successful space missions depend on careful design decisions, trade-offs, and risk management. We also hope it encourages curiosity about NASA’s open mission data and inspires players to learn more about space exploration! However, due to limited time, we have not yet had the opportunity to conduct a playtest.

Tools that were used for the project:

  • Materials = printed cards, printed "chip" components, dice, a printed board, clay(for the model orbiter), paint, brush, and scissors.
  • Hardware = Printer, camera, and microphone.
  • Software = Canva(design), Pinterest(design), Google(search engine), Claude AI(information gathering; to check data), and Microsoft Word(printing).

How is our project creative?

  • Players build their orbiter out of components with many varieties depending on their consideration, results, and management.
  • The payload has limited slots, a fixed budget, and the rule that instruments need power and a communication link makes the trade-offs of mission design the core of the game.
  • The event cards come from real spacecraft problems, for example: the Mars Climate Orbiter unit mismatch and the Galileo antenna that only partly opened. In the game, it's an event that players need to spend $300(game currency) to fix it.
  • Points depend on both arriving and the science points collected, so rushing with an empty spacecraft does not work.
  • Game improvements could be adding a digital rework, a landing module, a return mission, or a crewed version.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Accuracy: we scaled costs, masses (slot), and capacities from public data and rounded them so the game stays quick to learn. We state these simplifications in the presentation slides.
  • Fairness: We considered how a wide budget range could make the game overly dependent on luck. To improve fairness, we allowed players to make their own purchasing decisions and avoided overly dramatic differences in budgets, rules, and random events.
  • Accessibility: We chose low-cost materials and a completely non-digital format (coding) because we are all Junior High Schoolers and we have zero experience in coding :')
  • Sources: Almost every card includes its information source, and we avoided presenting scaled or simplified values as exact real-world measurements.
  • Time: we kept the rules to a small number of mechanics so the game could be built, tested(sadly didn't), and documented within the challenge time.  We apologize for any minor inconveniences, missing pieces, or anomalies. And we, as a team are doing our best! Thank you!
